The development of industrial parks and self-contained shopping centers has also been a powerful force for locating in or beyond suburban areas.
Some see the shift from the pull of ow land values to the push of urban problems:
Business is moving out for a variety of reasons. The explanation immediately after World War II was the attraction of cheap land in the suburbs, permitting single-story factories that were convenient for truck loading. In recent years, the motive is more push than pull. Executives complain about the abominable phone service in many cities, horrendous commuting conditions, rapidly rising crime. Even bomb threats are mentioned, when GT&E actually had a bomb go off in the building, the bosses lost no time in making the final decision to get the hell out. Then there are problems with the work force. Many young women seem to be avoiding the big cities, while young execs no longer consider a move to the New York office a promotion; indeed, they demand differential pay to cover the increased cost of living. There is also the desire to get away from it all, which was one of the big reasons why Xerox moved its top men from Rochester to pastoral Connecticut; the company president felt that they would get a better perspective of the whole company from the new, more isolated locale. But the biggest appeal of the suburbs, of course, is that much of the population, housing and development is there, or headed there (Cassidy, 1972).
Others see the lure of new kinds of prestige locations, closer to the preferred places of residence of the businessmen and decisionmakers. 30/
The forces that have caused decentralization and sprawl are expected to continue on a national basis and to overpower the efforts of some cities/regions to implement "no-growth" policies or to arrest further peripheral developments.
Population projections for the U.S. in 1985 and 2000 have been revised downward from estimates made in 1970 or earlier. For 1985, estimates range from about 237 to 257 million persons. For the year 2000, estimates range from 266 to 321 million persons. 31/ This would mean an increase over present U.S. population of about 22 to 42 million persons by 1985 and an approximate increase of 51 to 106 million persons by the year 2000. Where would these additional people live? The Bureau of Census believed at least two-thirds of them will be added to our metropolitan areas--assuming continuation of trends prior to 1970. 32/
